Marikana Decade [6210]

By: Viewfinder | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
we investigate how the lack of accountability following the Marikana massacre heralded a decade of police impunity within the police service

Unique Selling Point:
Access to documents showing that the police did not act against 77 police officers implicated in torture and assault after the Marikana massacre
Access to CCTV footage of killing by police officer

Summary:
The story is partly rooted in my exclusive access to disciplinary outcome documents following various police torture and assault cases in and around Marikana following the massacre. It shows that 77 police officers implicated in torture and assault of miners in the days after the massacre were unilaterally cleared of wrongdoing by the police. Then, I also bring in the telling case study of a police execution of a suspect in Durban which was incidentally also caught on camera (I have the CCTV footage in hand) in the weeks after the massacre. The cop - who was later found guilty of murder in court - was cleared by the police, and in stead promoted and given a medal. Taking Marikana as a baseline, then juxtaposing it to the Durban case study, I think a strong demonstration can be made that the Marikana fits within a continuum of police brutality and impunity which has continued unabated to the present day. The insert will end with an update of the Gabriels case, i.e. that he was subjected to a disciplinary hearing for alleged involvement in Adam Isaacs' murder in Athlone. But, that he was given a token sanction and will be back on the beat soon.

Further information:
Failure Marikana discipline heralded new decade of police impunity in SA
Tomorrow is the ten-year anniversary of the Marikana massacre. In the media and the public
discourse most reflections are bound to focus on the massacre itself and its aftermath.
Questions surrounding accountability for the killings, justice for the victims and compensation
for their widows and their families will dominate the narrative.
Yet, important nuance is lost when the massacre is becomes framed as a singular, historical
event. The Marikana massacre is in danger of becoming untethered from the often-lethal
violence and systemic non-accountability which underpinned it. And, the fact that the massacre
and its aftermath became a baseline for a new decade of police brutality and impunity in South
Africa.
Even the massacre itself did not exist in isolation from other – immediate – abuses of police
power. In the days and weeks after the massacre scores of miners were arrested, assaulted,
with some tortured mercilessly and charged with trumped up crimes. I have now gained
exclusive access to the police’s disciplinary outcome documents for 77 police officers
recommended for departmental action by the police watchdog for their alleged participation in
these assaults and torture cases. The complaints of more than 100 alleged victims are
summarised in these documents. In some cases they identified their alleged tormentors and
torturers by name.
Xolani Nzuza is one of the miners who says he experienced one of the worst bouts of torture in
this period. He has expressed willingness to receive me at Marikana, to be interviewed and to
connect us with other victims.
The disciplinary outcomes show that the police unilaterally cleared all 77 police officers
implicated in Nzuza and others’ assault and torture. None of these cases ever progressed to the
stage of disciplinary hearings. Similarly, there was never any disciplinary action for the massacre
itself.
But, one telling case study from Durban that occurred just weeks after the massacre in 2012
bears stark similarity to the massacre. In October 2012, police Captain Dumisani Dladla
exceuted an injured robbery suspect in cold blood on the streets of New Germany north of
Durban. He manipulated the crime scene – planting a gun next to the dead man’s hand – and
claimed self-defense. IPID’s investigators were harassed by the police and demonized when
they opened a murder case for investigation. Then, a few weeks later, CCTV footage emerged
showing that the killing was likely a murder, that the robbery suspect was not posing a threat.
Yet, even when confronted with this fact and the footage, a police disciplinary hearing still
found Captain Dladla not guilty. Instead of being disciplined in the months after the murder, he
received a rank promotion and a medal for distinguished service. Though he was later convicted
of murder in court, his sentence was so light that he was allowed to remain in the police and to
keep his firearm. I have access to: CCTV footage showing murder, court judgement finding
Dladla guilty of murder, disciplinary outcome showing that the police instead chose to acquit

him and other evidentiary material in the docket such as statements of witnesses and post-
mortem of victim, confirmation that he received a medal etc.
Data analyses and investigations done by Viewfinder has consistently shown how such
scenarios – where police officers remain on duty despite overwhelming criminal evidence
against them – is commonplace in South Africa. The case can easily be made, with reference to
expert knowledge and
In January and March Viewfinder exposed a problem police officer – Sgt Giovanni Gabriels from
Athlone – for his alleged participation and directing of the fatal torture of a suspect in January
2020. On the basis of that investigation police initiated a disciplinary hearing. Gabriels and a
colleague were found guilty of misconduct, but were only given a two month suspension. It is
understood that they are due to be back at work towards the end of this month. Witnesses who
were initially called to testify and arrived consistently at the hearing were dismissed and not
given the opportunity to speak. This provides a further opportunity for Carte Blanche to close
the loop on our investigation of Gabriels and to expose the police for its failure to hold him
accountable.
Interviews: Xolani Nzuza and potentially other miners (Marikana site visit), David Bruce
(Marikana panel of experts author who has made recommendations surrounding improved
police accountability), TBC commentator reflecting on the Durban police execution and CCTV
footage, family of Adam Isaacs and / or other witness who was due to testify against Gabriels,
but then was dismissed when he was given a light sanction. Police right-of-reply to be sought.
IPID invited to comment on the police’s failure to act against any of the 77 officers
recommended for discipline following Marikana torture / assault cases.

Two nights

Press Release:


This month marks ten years since the massacre at Marikana, where police shot and killed 34 striking miners. Despite the findings of an independent inquiry, no one within the police has been held accountable. Yet, evidence suggests police abuses didn’t end on the day of the shooting. In the weeks after the massacre, scores of miners were arrested, many claiming they were assaulted or tortured. Never-before-seen documents now reveal how police management unilaterally exonerated 77 officers implicated in these assaults and torture cases. Ten years on, there is every indication that the brutality at Marikana, and the lack of accountability that followed, is systemically rooted within the culture of the police service. No clearer is that demonstrated than in CCTV footage captured on the streets of New Germany north of Durban showing the premeditated killing of a defenceless suspect.

Script:


SCRIPTING

Voice over
The police’s massacre of 34 striking miners at Marikana in the North West on 16 August 2012 remains a blemish on the nation’s conscience.

This month saw the 10-year anniversary of the massacre commemorated at Marikana. Still, no one within the police has been held accountable for the killings.

Today silence has returned to the scene. Many miners still live in poverty, in shacks on the plains surrounding some of the country’s most lucrative platinum mines.

Xolani Nzuza was a strike leader who witnessed the deaths of some of his closest comrades.

MacFarlane
Bhut Xolani, it has been 10 years when you think of that day, when you just reflect on that day what comes to your mind?

Xolani
The time was around 4pm. We were sitting here.

Xolani
I was still up there on up the hill.The police had run to go block that side. Then it was just gunshots. So, when the gunshots started the workers came running back to this side.

You know I witnessed people being dragged around as if they were lifeless dogs. (Mac: eish my brother – use this to mask jump cut)

The other workers helped me to escape. They were concerned that no one would be able to testify, if we were all killed.

Voice over
In the aftermath of massacre, then President Jacob Zuma instituted a commission of inquiry chaired by retired Judge Ian Farlam.

Voice over
David Bruce is one of South Africa’s leading policing experts, and followed the proceedings closely.

MacFarlane
So in the immediate aftermath of Marikana, why do you think the police did not pursue any disciplinary investigations into some of the conduct of its own members?

David
Well, the short answer to that is that the SAPS took the position that it had done nothing wrong at Marikana. And throughout the commission of inquiry, that was the approach that they followed.

But then what you have at the commission is a large number of members of the SAPS is going to enormous lengths to mislead the commission as to what had happened at Marikana.

Voice over
The commission soon learned that the police’s attempted cover-up likely started within hours of the shootings. Photos submitted as exhibits to the commission suggested that weapons had been planted on the bodies of miners shot and killed at scene 2 of massacre, where police killed 17 people.

Voice over
One of the eventual outcomes of the Farlam Commission process was a series of recommendations that the police should initiate steps against senior police managers who lied under oath, against those who failed to probe the conduct of officers involved in the massacre, and against those officers implicated in the massacre itself.

In response to queries, the police said in a statement that it does not discuss labour related matters in public.

LINK
The atrocity of Marikana did not end with the shootings on 16 August 2012. In the days and weeks after the massacre, police arrested more than 200 miners, and detained them at stations dotted around the area. Many alleged that they were beaten and tortured while in custody.

Voice over
Xolani Nzuza believes that his arrest and torture in October 2012 was part of plot by police to silence him from testifying at the Farlam Commission.

Xolani
So when they eventually arrested me they took me to the police station at Marikana on the morning of the 17th of October


Xolani
They beat me to a pulp.They tortured me by cuffing my hands to a chair and then lifted the chair. Today it is still painful for me to lift anything heavy for even just five minutes. They cuffed my hands behind the chair and they kept stepping on the handcuffs.

They put a plastic bag over my head and poured water in and tied it here.

Mac
Do you remember their faces?

Xolani
Yes, I remember their faces. I know them.

Voice over
Police documents obtained by investigative journalism unit Viewfinder show that the Independent Police Investigative Directorate took statements from Xolani Nzuza and more than 150 miners who alleged police assaulted or tortured them in custody. The police watchdog IPID’s investigations identified 77 police officers implicated in these crimes, and made disciplinary recommendations against many of them

But police management refused to initiate a single disciplinary hearing and exonerated all of these officers. This echoed the lack of accountability for the massacre itself.

Police commissioner Fannie Masemola responded to queries that the decision to clear the 77 officers was based on “substantial evidence” and supported by the then-National Commissioner.

David
And so, in relation to Marikana, then you have a very clear message being sent out at the highest level of the SAPS that if you are implicated in the misuse of force. The leadership of the organization will cover for you. And so that message has permeated the organization.

LINK
Ten years on, the police have still not accounted for the massacre at Marikana. Every year since, police have killed hundreds of people. In an organisation that does not value transparency, who's to say that many such killings are not in fact cold blooded murders?

Voice over
This CCTV footage, captured in Durban a few weeks after the Marikana massacre, shows just how brazen such murders - and attempts at covering them up - can be.

Here a robbery suspect is fleeing the scene of a shoot-out with police, where an officer has been shot and killed, in the suburb of New Germany. The police are in pursuit. Also shot and badly injured the suspect is seen lying on the pavement soon there after. When he moves unexpectedly, police Captain Dumisani Dladla delivers a fatal gunshot to his head.

Sharmilla Williams was the IPID investigator who responded to the scene.

Sharmilla Williams
I remember there was a victim that was shot and killed by the police. When I arrived there, you know, people's attitudes towards me, they were a bit aggressive. But I still continue with my investigation, process the scene, you know, trying to figure out what transpired. And then there were things at the scene that did add up.

So, I insisted that they should actually open the murder charge.

Voice over
Williams was right to be suspicious. Captain Dladla is caught on camera as he plants a firearm on the pavement next to the victim's hand, shortly before she arrives on the scene.

Not knowing that his crime and attempted cover-up has been caught on camera, Captain Dladla would later claim to have acted in self-defense.

MacFarlane
A few weeks later, the CCTV footage of the incident appeared. How did that turn things around?

It was just frighteningly shocking to actually see that the police officer actually shot and killed in cold blood, that's what I saw on the CCTV, the suspect which surrendered at that stage and how they tampered with evidence at the scene, you know, to try and hide the crime.

Voice over
Despite the shocking CCTV footage and a recommendation from police watchdog IPID that Dladla be disciplined for his crimes, police management in KwaZulu Natal acquitted Captain Dladla in a disciplinary hearing. His employee profile shows that he was promoted in rank that same year, and given a medal for “an irreproachable character and exemplary conduct”.

Dladla was later convicted of murder in court. But, because he was not sentenced to prison, he remained in the police service.

Dladla
Unfortunately, sir, there is no statement that I am going to provide. You know, I am not allowed to talk to journalists. I am not the spokesperson. You can do that via the SAPS spokesperson.

Voice over
The police in KwaZulu Natal did not respond to our queries as to why Dladla was acquitted.

LINK
The shootings at Marikana and the murder of a suspect on the streets of New Germany in Durban may be ten years behind us. But, there is every indication that the culture of abuse and impunity remains entrenched within the police service today.

Voice over
In his inaugural address, in April, the country’s new police commissioner Fannie Masemola committed to address the low levels of “public trust” and the issue of “integrity” within police.

But this rhetoric is not new.

In the police’s annual report for the year of the Marikana massacre, police commissioner Riah Phiyega said that “integrity” and “discipline” were fundamental to police work.

In the decade since, the police have been accused of thousands of killings and tens of thousands of acts of brutality.

Yet, almost none of these cases have led to disciplinary convictions, much less dismissals.

As happened in response to the Marikana torture cases, police management still tends towards overruling watchdog recommendations to exonerate officers implicated in crimes.

Masemola’s office did not respond to queries about how he intended to stem the tide of impunity.

Masemola’s office responded to queries, saying that he intends “deal decisively with complaints against the Police” through the police’s “Inspectorate”, “Community Imbizos” and “awareness campaigns” for officers “on the importance of ethical conduct and integrity”.

He is “applying his mind towards enhancing the current disciplinary system.”


David
Addressing the legacy of Marikana is something that is unavoidable for the SAPS, if it wants to establish itself as a police service, which is trusted by members of the public.


Xolani
I wanted all of them to be lined up, so that I can identify them and say: “it was this one and this one”. They did not allow for that.

It is so heavy for me to speak about this, because there has been no action taken against the police. I have not heard of any police officers that were arrested

So my brother, I don’t trust the police at all.

The leadership of the organization will cover for you. And so that message has permeated the organization. LINK Ten years on, the police have still not accounted for the massacre at Marikana. Every year since, police have killed hundreds of people. In an organisation that does not value transparency, who's to say that many such killings are not in fact cold blooded murders? Voice over This CCTV footage, captured in Durban a few weeks after the Marikana massacre, shows just how brazen such murders - and attempts at covering them up - can be. Here a robbery suspect is fleeing the scene of a shoot-out with police, where an officer has been shot and killed, in the suburb of New Germany. The police are in pursuit. Also shot and badly injured the suspect is seen lying on the pavement soon there after. When he moves unexpectedly, police Captain Dumisani Dladla delivers a fatal gunshot to his head. Sharmilla Williams was the IPID investigator who responded to the scene. Sharmilla Williams I remember there was a victim that was shot and killed by the police. When I arrived there, you know, people's attitudes towards me, they were a bit aggressive. But I still continue with my investigation, process the scene, you know, trying to figure out what transpired. And then there were things at the scene that did add up. So, I insisted that they should actually open the murder charge. Voice over Williams was right to be suspicious. Captain Dladla is caught on camera as he plants a firearm on the pavement next to the victim's hand, shortly before she arrives on the scene. Not knowing that his crime and attempted cover-up has been caught on camera, Captain Dladla would later claim to have acted in self-defense. MacFarlane A few weeks later, the CCTV footage of the incident appeared. How did that turn things around? It was just frighteningly shocking to actually see that the police officer actually shot and killed in cold blood, that's what I saw on the CCTV, the suspect which surrendered at that stage and how they tampered with evidence at the scene, you know, to try and hide the crime. Voice over Despite the shocking CCTV footage and a recommendation from police watchdog IPID that Dladla be disciplined for his crimes, police management in KwaZulu Natal acquitted Captain Dladla in a disciplinary hearing. His employee profile shows that he was promoted in rank that same year, and given a medal for “an irreproachable character and exemplary conduct”. Dladla was later convicted of murder in court. But, because he was not sentenced to prison, he remained in the police service. Dladla Unfortunately, sir, there is no statement that I am going to provide. You know, I am not allowed to talk to journalists. I am not the spokesperson. You can do that via the SAPS spokesperson. Voice over The police in KwaZulu Natal did not respond to our queries as to why Dladla was acquitted. LINK The shootings at Marikana and the murder of a suspect on the streets of New Germany in Durban may be ten years behind us. But, there is every indication that the culture of abuse and impunity remains entrenched within the police service today. Voice over In his inaugural address, in April, the country’s new police commissioner Fannie Masemola committed to address the low levels of “public trust” and the issue of “integrity” within police. But this rhetoric is not new. In the police’s annual report for the year of the Marikana massacre, police commissioner Riah Phiyega said that “integrity” and “discipline” were fundamental to police work. In the decade since, the police have been accused of thousands of killings and tens of thousands of acts of brutality. Yet, almost none of these cases have led to disciplinary convictions, much less dismissals. As happened in response to the Marikana torture cases, police management still tends towards overruling watchdog recommendations to exonerate officers implicated in crimes. Masemola’s office did not respond to queries about how he intended to stem the tide of impunity. Masemola’s office responded to queries, saying that he intends “deal decisively with complaints against the Police” through the police’s “Inspectorate”, “Community Imbizos” and “awareness campaigns” for officers “on the importance of ethical conduct and integrity”. He is “applying his mind towards enhancing the current disciplinary system.” David Addressing the legacy of Marikana is something that is unavoidable for the SAPS, if it wants to establish itself as a police service, which is trusted by members of the public. Xolani I wanted all of them to be lined up, so that I can identify them and say: “it was this one and this one”. They did not allow for that. It is so heavy for me to speak about this, because there has been no action taken against the police. I have not heard of any police officers that were arrested So my brother, I don’t trust the police at all.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): we investigate how the lack of accountability following the Marikana massacre heralded a decade of police impunity within the police service
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Access to documents showing that the police did not act against 77 police officers implicated in torture and assault after the Marikana massacre Access to CCTV footage of killing by police officer
metadata.Summary: The story is partly rooted in my exclusive access to disciplinary outcome documents following various police torture and assault cases in and around Marikana following the massacre. It shows that 77 police officers implicated in torture and assault of miners in the days after the massacre were unilaterally cleared of wrongdoing by the police. Then, I also bring in the telling case study of a police execution of a suspect in Durban which was incidentally also caught on camera (I have the CCTV footage in hand) in the weeks after the massacre. The cop - who was later found guilty of murder in court - was cleared by the police, and in stead promoted and given a medal. Taking Marikana as a baseline, then juxtaposing it to the Durban case study, I think a strong demonstration can be made that the Marikana fits within a continuum of police brutality and impunity which has continued unabated to the present day. The insert will end with an update of the Gabriels case, i.e. that he was subjected to a disciplinary hearing for alleged involvement in Adam Isaacs' murder in Athlone. But, that he was given a token sanction and will be back on the beat soon.
metadata.Further information: Failure Marikana discipline heralded new decade of police impunity in SA Tomorrow is the ten-year anniversary of the Marikana massacre. In the media and the public discourse most reflections are bound to focus on the massacre itself and its aftermath. Questions surrounding accountability for the killings, justice for the victims and compensation for their widows and their families will dominate the narrative. Yet, important nuance is lost when the massacre is becomes framed as a singular, historical event. The Marikana massacre is in danger of becoming untethered from the often-lethal violence and systemic non-accountability which underpinned it. And, the fact that the massacre and its aftermath became a baseline for a new decade of police brutality and impunity in South Africa. Even the massacre itself did not exist in isolation from other – immediate – abuses of police power. In the days and weeks after the massacre scores of miners were arrested, assaulted, with some tortured mercilessly and charged with trumped up crimes. I have now gained exclusive access to the police’s disciplinary outcome documents for 77 police officers recommended for departmental action by the police watchdog for their alleged participation in these assaults and torture cases. The complaints of more than 100 alleged victims are summarised in these documents. In some cases they identified their alleged tormentors and torturers by name. Xolani Nzuza is one of the miners who says he experienced one of the worst bouts of torture in this period. He has expressed willingness to receive me at Marikana, to be interviewed and to connect us with other victims. The disciplinary outcomes show that the police unilaterally cleared all 77 police officers implicated in Nzuza and others’ assault and torture. None of these cases ever progressed to the stage of disciplinary hearings. Similarly, there was never any disciplinary action for the massacre itself. But, one telling case study from Durban that occurred just weeks after the massacre in 2012 bears stark similarity to the massacre. In October 2012, police Captain Dumisani Dladla exceuted an injured robbery suspect in cold blood on the streets of New Germany north of Durban. He manipulated the crime scene – planting a gun next to the dead man’s hand – and claimed self-defense. IPID’s investigators were harassed by the police and demonized when they opened a murder case for investigation. Then, a few weeks later, CCTV footage emerged showing that the killing was likely a murder, that the robbery suspect was not posing a threat. Yet, even when confronted with this fact and the footage, a police disciplinary hearing still found Captain Dladla not guilty. Instead of being disciplined in the months after the murder, he received a rank promotion and a medal for distinguished service. Though he was later convicted of murder in court, his sentence was so light that he was allowed to remain in the police and to keep his firearm. I have access to: CCTV footage showing murder, court judgement finding Dladla guilty of murder, disciplinary outcome showing that the police instead chose to acquit him and other evidentiary material in the docket such as statements of witnesses and post- mortem of victim, confirmation that he received a medal etc. Data analyses and investigations done by Viewfinder has consistently shown how such scenarios – where police officers remain on duty despite overwhelming criminal evidence against them – is commonplace in South Africa. The case can easily be made, with reference to expert knowledge and In January and March Viewfinder exposed a problem police officer – Sgt Giovanni Gabriels from Athlone – for his alleged participation and directing of the fatal torture of a suspect in January 2020. On the basis of that investigation police initiated a disciplinary hearing. Gabriels and a colleague were found guilty of misconduct, but were only given a two month suspension. It is understood that they are due to be back at work towards the end of this month. Witnesses who were initially called to testify and arrived consistently at the hearing were dismissed and not given the opportunity to speak. This provides a further opportunity for Carte Blanche to close the loop on our investigation of Gabriels and to expose the police for its failure to hold him accountable. Interviews: Xolani Nzuza and potentially other miners (Marikana site visit), David Bruce (Marikana panel of experts author who has made recommendations surrounding improved police accountability), TBC commentator reflecting on the Durban police execution and CCTV footage, family of Adam Isaacs and / or other witness who was due to testify against Gabriels, but then was dismissed when he was given a light sanction. Police right-of-reply to be sought. IPID invited to comment on the police’s failure to act against any of the 77 officers recommended for discipline following Marikana torture / assault cases.
